About me

About me

I graduate in November 2026 with a Master of Business from the University of Queensland, where I've specialised in Information Systems and Marketing. Before that, my undergraduate studies covered economics and international business.

I chose that mix on purpose. I've always been interested in the space between the business side and the tech side, and business analysis and consulting are where those two meet. I enjoy talking to the people doing the work, understanding what's getting in their way, and then digging into the data to help find a better way of doing it.

My internship at Chatstat confirmed it for me. I spent eight weeks helping a team work out whether their AI tools were actually working, and that's the kind of work I want to keep doing.

Chatstat · AI Implementation Analyst · Jun–Aug 2026

Deciding which AI agents were ready to scale

BaseliningKPI designAdoption analysisExcel
The problem
Four AI agents were being piloted with no agreed way to tell whether any of them were working.
What I built
Operational baselines for three agents, a pre-pilot metrics pack with primary, secondary and guardrail metrics and go / redesign / discontinue thresholds, weekly measurement workbooks, adoption analyses and a mid-cycle operations report.
What it showed
All four agents saved a lot of time, but output quality only held up for two of them. I presented the findings at Demo Day at the end of Cycle 1.

University of Queensland

A business model for a property manager

Pivot tablesMarket benchmarkingScenario analysisProfit modellingMap visualisation
The problem
Yuan Yards, a Brisbane property manager with five offices, needed to know where its rents sat against the market, how rent varied across its offices, and whether short-stay rentals were worth adding.
What I built
A suburb-level benchmark of the portfolio's median rents against ABS data shown on a 3D map, a pivot table breaking down rent by dwelling type, suburb and office, and a short-stay profit model tested across 12 scenarios.
What it showed
Indooroopilly brings in over half of all rent received. In the short-stay model, staffing load moved profit far more than bookings did: doubling it cut profit from about $30.5K to $6.6K.

Seeing who defaults on a loan

Power BIData cleaningDashboard design
The problem
A bank wanted to understand which customer and financial traits go with loan default.
What I built
After cleaning the data, I built two interactive dashboards, one on customer profile and one on financial and credit risk, with filters for state, income and gender.
What it showed
Default risk comes from several factors together. Income, education and past bankruptcy mattered most, while state and gender made little difference.

University of Queensland

Redesigning a repair-parts warehouse process

BPMNAs-is / to-beProcess improvementAutomation
The problem
FlowForge Solutions, a repair-parts warehouse, handles around 160 repair requests a day. Requests arrived by mail and email and were matched by hand, saved to a shared drive and retyped into a database, with paper double-checks along the way.
What I built
As-is and to-be BPMN models of the whole operation, split into 10 sub-processes covering receiving requests, dispatching spares, triage, repairs, returns and closing out the day, with each role in its own lane.
What it showed
Nine improvements across automation, removing tasks, re-ordering steps, communication and staffing. For example, an online request form replaces matching mail with email and checks each part against the Parts Type List up front, so irrelevant parts are rejected before any intake work starts.
10sub-processes mapped
9improvements proposed
~160repair requests a day
University of Queensland

Designing a childcare management system

RequirementsUser storiesAcceptance criteriaUML
The problem
A childcare centre needed one system for attendance, family records, daily care tasks, room ratios and Montessori learning progress, while staying compliant with Queensland staffing ratios.
What I did
Wrote five functional and five non-functional requirements as user stories with acceptance criteria, then modelled the system in UML: a use case diagram, two activity diagrams, two sequence diagrams, a state diagram and a class diagram.
Key design choices
The system checks who has signed in at the 9am roll call, so staff don't have to, and offers absent children's spots to the waitlist straight away. Welfare tasks like meals and sleep are kept separate from learning records, which keeps the design easy to extend.
10requirements written
7UML diagrams
6rooms with QLD ratios built in
University of Queensland · Summer Research Assistant · Jan–Mar 2026

How digital technology drove Domino's growth

Systematic screeningFactivaNVivoQualitative codingTechnology mapping
The problem
A Digital Strategy & Transformation project needed to show how Domino's used digital technology to grow, without changing the core product itself.
What I did
Screened over 1,380 secondary sources in Factiva to extend a dataset of Domino's digital evolution from 2018 to 2022, then coded the material in NVivo to find patterns in how technology removed friction for operations and customers.
What it showed
Read through a friction-reduction lens, Domino's digital platforms acted as growth catalysts on their own. I added and validated more than 20 new technology properties and partnerships in the project's technology map, keeping only global, scalable innovations.

20+technologies validated
